title: Windowing Large Lists
description: Master windowing and virtualization techniques to render large datasets efficiently with React Query.

data.text: Rendering thousands of rows in a table or list kills performance because the DOM has to manage every node. **Windowing** (also called virtualization) renders only the visible subset of rows and reuses DOM nodes as the user scrolls. When combined with React Query, windowing keeps the data cached and ready while the UI stays buttery smooth.

A list of 10,000 items means 10,000 DOM elements. Each element carries event listeners, styles, and memory overhead. Even with React's reconciliation, the initial paint and subsequent scroll events become janky. Windowing solves this by rendering only ~20-30 items at a time, regardless of total data size.

data.title: Do not window small lists
data.text: Windowing adds complexity. Only apply it when you expect more than 100-200 visible items. For smaller lists, standard mapping is faster and simpler.

terms.definition: Rendering only the visible portion of a list, recycling DOM nodes as the user scrolls.
A virtualization technique that renders a sliding window of items matching the viewport size.
Reusing existing DOM elements for new data items instead of creating and destroying them.

data.text: Libraries like `react-window` and `react-virtuoso` handle the math of viewport calculation and DOM recycling. The key integration point is feeding the cached query data into the windowed list. React Query fetches and caches the full dataset; the windowing library handles rendering.

data.text: Some lists have rows of varying height. `react-window` provides `VariableSizeList` for this scenario. You must measure or estimate row heights upfront. Alternatively, `react-virtuoso` auto-detects row sizes, making it a better choice for dynamic content like chat messages or cards with multiline text.

cards.title: react-window
cards.description: Lightweight, battle-tested windowing library by Brian Vaughn.
cons: Requires manual row height for variable lists

cards.title: react-virtuoso
cards.description: Feature-rich virtualization with automatic sizing and follow-output.

cards.title: tanstack-virtual
cards.description: Headless virtualizer from TanStack. Framework-agnostic core.

data.text: When you combine infinite queries with windowing, you get an infinite scroll that stays performant. React Query's `useInfiniteQuery` fetches pages; the windowing library renders only what is visible. The integration requires calculating total item count from `data.pages` and flattening the nested page structure.

data.title: Infinite scroll with react-window
data.content: Combining useInfiniteQuery with a virtualized list for smooth infinite scroll

items.text: Measure or estimate row heights before choosing a library
items.hint: Variable-size lists need accurate measurements for smooth scrolling.

items.text: Keep React Query fetching logic separate from windowing rendering logic
items.hint: Query fetches pages; windowing renders what is visible.

items.text: Flatten infinite query pages before passing to the list component
items.hint: useInfiniteQuery returns nested pages; windowing expects a flat array.

items.text: Trigger fetchNextPage when the user is within 5-10 items of the end
items.hint: Fetching too early wastes requests; too late causes visible loading.

items.text: Show a loading indicator at the bottom when fetching the next page
items.hint: Users need feedback that more content is coming.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Windowing renders only visible items, not the full dataset
Pair react-window or react-virtuoso with useQuery or useInfiniteQuery
Flatten infinite query pages before feeding them to the list
Choose react-virtuoso when row heights are dynamic
data.takeaway: Windowing keeps large lists performant by trading DOM nodes for scroll math.
